title: Python Foundations for Data Science
subtitle: Learn the Python data scientists use every day: the IPython shell, built-in data structures, functions and lambdas, Jupyter notebooks, and tidy scripts that cope with messy data.
outcomes: Explore data interactively in IPython, using its help, history, Tab completion and magic commands
Choose between lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets to store, count, group and de-duplicate records
Write decisions, loops, comprehensions and functions, including lambdas as sort keys, to clean and summarise data
Build Jupyter notebooks that mix code, Markdown, charts and magic commands, run cleanly from top to bottom and export to share
Turn notebook code into a documented command-line script that handles bad data and errors, tracked in Git
prerequisites: None: it starts from zero and needs only school maths. You need a computer with Python 3 (python.org has installers); the labs install IPython, JupyterLab and matplotlib into a virtual environment, and module 5 uses Git. Python Programming with PyCharm teaches the language in an IDE, with debugging and testing; this course teaches it the way data scientists work, in IPython and Jupyter, so the two go well together.
description:
Data scientists spend their days in Python, but not the way most programming courses teach it. They explore in an interactive shell, keep their analyses in notebooks, and turn what works into scripts that run every week. This course teaches the Python you need for that, from zero, on the kind of data a farm co-operative collects: weather station logs and grain deliveries (all made up for the course). You'll start in IPython, the enhanced interactive shell, learning Python's syntax, its types and their surprises, such as why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3. Then you'll learn Python's four built-in collections and when to use each: lists for ordered records, tuples for fixed ones, dictionaries for look-ups, counts and groups, and sets for unique values and quick comparisons.

Next come decisions, loops, comprehensions and functions, including lambdas as sort keys, which you'll use to parse and clean messy readings. In JupyterLab you'll build a notebook that mixes code, Markdown, a chart and magic commands, and export it to share. Finally you'll turn your code into a command-line script with modules, docstrings, error handling and logging, and keep its history in Git. Every module has a hands-on lab with exact results to check, and the capstone is a script that turns a messy season of grain deliveries into a clean file and a report, using nothing but Python's built-in tools. It's the foundation for Data Wrangling with pandas and NumPy.

modules.title: Introduction to Python and IPython
modules.summary: Set up Python and IPython in a virtual environment, learn how Python code is laid out, and meet its basic types, with IPython's help, history and magic commands to explore as you go.

lessons.title: Python for data work, and the IPython shell
objectives: Explain where Python fits in data science and what an interactive shell is for
Install IPython in a virtual environment and use its prompts, help and history
key_points: Python is a general-purpose language and one of the most widely used for data work, thanks to libraries such as NumPy, pandas, matplotlib and scikit-learn. An interpreter runs the code, so you can try a line and see its result straight away.

A REPL (read, evaluate, print loop) runs each line you type and shows the result. IPython is an enhanced one: numbered In and Out prompts, Tab completion, syntax colouring and magic commands that start with %.

Install IPython into a project's virtual environment: create it with python3 -m venv .venv (py -m venv .venv on Windows), activate it, run python -m pip install ipython, then start the shell with ipython; exit leaves it.
Help is built in: name? shows an object's signature and docstring, name?? also shows its source code when it's written in Python, and Tab completes names, attributes and file paths.
IPython keeps your history: _ is the last result, Out[n] (or _n) the result of prompt n, the Up arrow and Ctrl+R recall earlier lines, and %history lists what you've typed.
A line starting with ! runs a shell command, such as !ls or !dir, and %run script.py runs a file inside the session, so the variables it creates are still there afterwards.

lessons.title: Syntax, indentation and variables
objectives: Read and write Python statements, comments and indented blocks
Create variables and explain what dynamic typing means
key_points: A Python program is a series of statements, usually one per line; everything after a # on a line is a comment, which Python ignores.

Indentation defines blocks: the lines indented under a line that ends in a colon, such as an if or a for, belong to it. Use four spaces per level; a missing or inconsistent indent raises an IndentationError.

A variable is a name bound to a value with =, as in rain_mm = 3.8. Names are case-sensitive, can't start with a digit or be a keyword such as for or if, and by convention use lower case with underscores.
Python is dynamically typed: values have types but names don't, so a name can be rebound to a value of another type, and type(x) tells you what x holds right now.
Assignment never copies a value: b = a makes b a second name for the same object, which matters as soon as the object can change, as a list can.
Augmented assignment updates a variable in place, as in total += rain_mm, and a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line.

lessons.title: Numbers, text and truth: the basic types
objectives: Use int, float, str, bool and None, and convert between them
Avoid the classic surprises of float arithmetic, division and truthiness
key_points: int holds whole numbers of any size and float holds decimals. / always gives a float (7 / 2 is 3.5), // gives floor division, which rounds down (7 // 2 is 3 but -7 // 2 is -4), and % the remainder.
Floats are stored in binary, so most decimals are close approximations: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with math.isclose() rather than ==, and round them only for display.
str holds text and can't be changed in place: methods such as strip(), lower(), title(), replace() and split() return new strings. An f-string formats values, as in f'{mean:.1f} C' or f'{total:,}'.
bool is True or False; comparisons produce one, and and, or and not combine them. In a condition, 0, 0.0, empty strings, empty collections and None count as false, and nearly everything else as true.
None means no value, which is how plain Python usually marks a missing reading; test for it with x is None, not x == None.
Converting text is often the first step with data: float('24.6') and int('17') work, int('3.5') raises a ValueError, and bool('False') is True, because any non-empty string is.

modules.title: Built-in Data Structures
modules.summary: Store and organise records with Python's four built-in collections, lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets, and learn which one fits each job, from counting and grouping to removing duplicates.

lessons.title: Lists: ordered, changeable sequences
objectives: Create, index, slice and change lists
Explain when two names share one list, and copy a list when they shouldn't
key_points: A list holds items in order and can change after it's made: readings = [24.6, 19.0, 31.2]. It can mix types, but a list of one kind of item is far easier to work with.

Indexes start at 0 and negative ones count from the end: readings[0] is the first item and readings[-1] the last. A slice such as readings[1:3] is a new list of items 1 and 2, because the stop index is left out.
Lists change in place: append() adds one item, extend() adds several, insert() puts one at a position, pop() removes and returns one, and remove() deletes the first item equal to a value.
sorted(readings) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original alone; readings.sort() sorts the list itself and returns None, so writing new = readings.sort() is a bug.
len(), sum(), min() and max() work on a list of numbers, and x in readings checks membership by looking at the items one by one, which gets slow for long lists.
b = a gives the same list a second name, so a change made through b shows up in a. a.copy(), list(a) or a[:] make a new list; these copies are shallow, so lists nested inside are still shared.

lessons.title: Tuples and unpacking: fixed records
objectives: Use tuples for records whose fields belong together
Unpack tuples into names, including in for loops
key_points: A tuple is an ordered sequence that can't be changed once made, written with commas and usually brackets: delivery = (1001, 'Prairie Rose Farm', 'canola', 21.4).
Unpacking gives a tuple's items names in one step: ticket, farm, crop, tonnes = delivery. The number of names must match, unless one name takes the rest with a star, as in first, *rest = readings.
Unpacking works in for loops too: for ticket, farm, crop, tonnes in deliveries: gives each field a name, which reads far better than d[0] and d[3].
Tuples are hashable when their items are, so they can be dictionary keys or set members, such as a (farm, crop) pair used as a key; lists can't.
A function can return several values as a tuple, as in return low, high; enumerate() and zip() also produce tuples, which loops usually unpack.
collections.namedtuple gives a tuple's fields names: Delivery = namedtuple('Delivery', ['ticket', 'farm', 'crop', 'tonnes']), and then d.tonnes reads better than d[3].

lessons.title: Dictionaries: look-ups, counts and groups
objectives: Store and look up values by key
Count and group records with dictionaries, Counter and defaultdict
key_points: A dictionary maps unique keys to values: moisture = {'canola': 9.8, 'wheat': 13.1}. moisture['wheat'] looks a value up and raises KeyError if the key is missing; moisture.get('oats') returns None, or a default you pass, instead.
Keys must be hashable, such as strings, numbers or tuples of them, while values can be anything. Dictionaries keep keys in the order they were added, which Python has guaranteed since version 3.7.
Loop over keys and values together with .items(); .keys() and .values() give each on its own. Assigning to a key adds it, or replaces its value if it's already there.

Counting: counts[crop] = counts.get(crop, 0) + 1, or let collections.Counter do it, with most_common(n) for the top n. Grouping: with groups = defaultdict(list), groups[crop].append(ticket) creates each list the first time it's needed.

Tabular data comes in two shapes: a list of dictionaries, one per record, or a dictionary of lists, one per column. JSON maps onto both (json.load reads a file, json.dumps writes text), and pandas can build a table from either.

lessons.title: Sets: unique values and fast membership
objectives: Remove duplicates and test membership with sets
Compare two collections with set operations
key_points: A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable items: set(['wheat', 'oats', 'wheat']) has two members. {} is an empty dictionary, so an empty set is written set().
Turning a list into a set removes its duplicates but loses its order; list(dict.fromkeys(items)) removes them and keeps the first of each in order.

x in a_set takes about the same time however big the set is, because sets use hashing like dictionary keys, while x in a_list checks item by item. Convert a long list you search again and again into a set.

Set operations compare collections: a | b is the union, a & b the intersection, a - b what's in a but not b, and a ^ b what's in one but not both. members - delivered finds members who delivered nothing.
A set has no positions, so s[0] fails and a printed set can list its items in any order; use sorted(s) when the order matters.
A frozenset is a set that can't change, so it can be a dictionary key or a member of another set.

modules.title: Control Flow and Functions
modules.summary: Make decisions with if, elif and else, repeat work with loops and comprehensions, and package your logic in functions and lambdas that parse, clean and summarise messy readings.

lessons.title: Decisions: if, elif and else
objectives: Write conditions that choose between several actions
Handle missing values and boundary cases explicitly
key_points: if runs its block when its condition is true; elif adds more conditions, checked in order; else catches whatever is left. Only the first true branch runs, so put the highest threshold or the most specific case first.
Comparisons (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=) give True or False and can be chained: 10 <= temp < 20 is true when temp is at least 10 and below 20.
and, or and not combine conditions. and stops at the first false part and or at the first true one, so temp is not None and temp > 30 never compares None with a number.
Test for a missing value with is None: if temp: would also treat a genuine reading of 0.0 as missing.
A conditional expression chooses between two values in one line: label = 'dry' if rain == 0 else 'wet'. Anything longer reads better as a full if statement.

lessons.title: Loops and comprehensions
objectives: Repeat work over data with for and while loops
Build lists, sets and dictionaries with comprehensions
key_points: A for loop runs its block once for each item of a sequence, set, dictionary or file. range(n) gives 0 to n - 1, enumerate() adds a counter to each item and zip() walks through two sequences side by side.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays true, so something inside it must eventually make the condition false; it suits loops with no fixed number of rounds.
break leaves a loop at once, for example when the first match is found, and continue skips to the next item, for example past a bad record.
The accumulator pattern builds a result as a loop runs: set total = 0 or found = [] before the loop and update it inside.
A comprehension builds a collection in one expression: [d['max'] for d in days if d['max'] is not None] makes a list, {d['crop'] for d in loads} a set and {k: v for k, v in pairs} a dictionary.
Don't add items to a list or remove them while looping over it, because items get skipped; loop over a copy, or build a new list with a comprehension.

lessons.title: Functions: def, parameters and return values
objectives: Define functions with parameters, defaults and return values
Write small functions that each clean or check one thing
key_points: def defines a function: a name, parameters in brackets and an indented body. return sends a value back to the caller, and a function that finishes without return gives None.
Arguments can be passed by position or by name, and parameters can have default values: def parse_float(text, missing=('', 'n/a')) works as parse_float(' 3.8 ') or with missing= given.

Names created inside a function are local: they disappear when it returns and don't change names outside it. Pass data in as arguments and get results out with return rather than using global variables.
A function that depends only on its arguments and returns a result, without printing or changing anything else, is easy to test and reuse: parse_float(' 24.6 ') should always give 24.6.
A docstring, the string on the first line of the body, says what the function does, what it takes and what it returns; help(parse_float) and parse_float? show it.
*args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs extra keyword arguments into a dictionary, which is how print() accepts any number of values.

lessons.title: Lambdas and functions as values
objectives: Pass functions as arguments, for example as sort keys
Write lambda functions, and know when def is clearer
key_points: Functions are values: they can be stored in variables or collections and passed to other functions, such as sorted(), max() and min(), which take a key function.
A lambda is a small anonymous function written as one expression: lambda d: d['rain'] takes d and returns its rain. It can't contain statements such as if blocks or loops.
key= decides what is compared: sorted(days, key=lambda d: d['rain'], reverse=True) puts the wettest day first, and max(deliveries, key=lambda d: d[3]) finds the biggest load.

A key can return a tuple to sort by several things: key=lambda d: (d['crop'], -d['tonnes']) sorts by crop, then by tonnes from largest to smallest. Python's sort is stable, so ties keep their original order.
map(f, items) applies a function to every item and filter(f, items) keeps the items for which it returns true; both give lazy iterators, and a comprehension is usually clearer.
When a lambda grows long or needs a name to be understood, write it with def instead; PEP 8, Python's style guide, advises against assigning a lambda to a name.

lessons.title: JupyterLab, notebooks and kernels
objectives: Start JupyterLab and create a notebook
Run cells in command and edit mode, and explain what the kernel keeps between cells
key_points: A Jupyter notebook (an .ipynb file) is a document of cells, code with its output and Markdown text, saved as JSON. JupyterLab, installed with pip install jupyterlab and started with jupyter lab, is the browser-based environment for working with notebooks.
Each notebook is connected to a kernel, a running Python process (IPython, in fact) that runs the code cells and keeps every variable between them until it's restarted.
Shift+Enter runs a cell and moves to the next. The number in brackets beside a code cell shows the order in which cells ran, and the value of a cell's last expression is displayed below it.

Cells can be run in any order, so a notebook's results can depend on cells you've since changed or deleted. Restarting the kernel and running all cells checks that it works from top to bottom before you trust or share it.
Edit mode (Enter) is for typing in a cell and command mode (Esc) for working on cells: A and B insert a cell above or below, M and Y turn it into Markdown or code, and pressing D twice deletes it.

modules.title: Python Scripting Lab
modules.summary: Turn exploratory code into a script you can rerun and share: functions in modules, a command-line interface, error handling and logging for bad data, docstrings and comments, and a history in Git.

lessons.title: From notebook to script: modules and a main function
objectives: Structure a script with imports, functions and a main() guarded by __name__
Import your own modules and read command-line arguments
key_points: A script is a .py file run with python script.py. A tidy one has its imports at the top, then constants, then functions that each do one job, and a main() function that ties them together.
Code under if __name__ == '__main__': runs only when the file is run directly, not when another file imports it, so one file can be both a script and a module.
Any .py file in the same folder is a module you can import: import weather_tools, then call weather_tools.parse_float(). Modules keep each file short and let notebooks and scripts share code.

argparse turns command-line arguments into variables: parser.add_argument('path') adds a required argument and add_argument('--station', default='North Field') an option, and --help is written for you.

The csv module reads and writes CSV files: csv.DictReader gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header, and csv.DictWriter writes dictionaries out. Open the files with newline='' and encoding='utf-8'.

lessons.title: Errors and exceptions: scripts that survive bad data
objectives: Catch and raise exceptions to deal with bad input
Report problems with logging and exit codes
key_points: When something fails, Python raises an exception, such as ValueError for text that isn't a number, KeyError for a missing key or FileNotFoundError for a missing file. If nothing catches it, the script stops with a traceback.

try runs code that might fail and except SomeError handles that error; else runs only if nothing failed and finally runs either way. Catch the specific errors you expect, never everything with a bare except.
With messy data, decide what each problem deserves: skip and count a bad row, keep a gap as None, or stop the run. Whatever you choose, report it, so nobody mistakes cleaned data for complete data.
raise ValueError('missing value for rain_mm') signals a problem in your own function, with a message that says what went wrong; the caller can catch it like any other exception.

The logging module reports progress and problems: logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) sets it up, and log.warning() and log.error() write messages labelled with their level to the error stream, stderr, apart from the results.
A script reports success or failure through its exit code: 0 means it worked, and sys.exit(1), or sys.exit(main()) with main() returning 1, tells the shell or a scheduler that it failed.

lessons.title: Docstrings, comments and version control with Git
objectives: Document a script with docstrings, comments and a README
Track a script's changes with Git: init, add, commit, log and diff
key_points: Comments (#) explain why the code does something that isn't obvious, such as a business rule; the code itself should show what it does. A comment that repeats the code adds nothing and goes out of date.

A docstring, the triple-quoted string at the top of a module or function, describes its purpose, arguments, return value and errors. help() and IPython's ? show it, and PEP 257 sets out the conventions.

Git records snapshots of a project, called commits: git init starts a repository, git add stages changes, git commit -m 'message' records them, git status and git diff show what has changed, and git log --oneline lists the history.
Commit small, related changes with messages that say what changed and why, such as Skip rows with missing rain values, so every step can be inspected or undone.
A .gitignore file keeps things out of the repository: the virtual environment (.venv/), __pycache__/, .ipynb_checkpoints/, and data files that are large or private.
Notebooks are JSON with their outputs inside, so their diffs are hard to read; clear the outputs before committing, or keep reusable code in .py files, which diff cleanly.

def load_readings(path):
    """Read the CSV file at path. Return the readings that parse, and how many rows were skipped."""
    days, skipped = [], 0
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:

project.title: Data Analysis Scripting Lab: clean a season of grain deliveries
project.brief: A farm co-operative's grain elevator has exported a season of deliveries (made-up data) to deliveries_raw.csv, and it's messy: some rows were exported twice; farm and crop names are typed in several ways, including the aliases Prairie Rose, N. Star Grain and Birch Ck Farm; weights are in tonnes (21.4 or 21.4 t) or kilograms (21400 kg or 21,400 kg); moisture is sometimes blank, n/a or written with a % sign; dates are written 2025-08-14 or 14/08/2025; and a few rows are impossible. Write a Python script, using only the standard library and built-in data structures (no pandas), that reads the file, cleans it and writes clean_deliveries.csv, rejected.csv (each rejected row with its reason) and report.md, a summary for the co-operative's board. The rules: remove exact duplicate rows; give every farm one spelling (strip, title case, then the aliases) and every crop one (strip, lower case); convert weights to tonnes; keep missing moisture empty rather than inventing a value; write dates as YYYY-MM-DD; and reject rows with no weight, a weight of 0 or less or over 45 t, or moisture over 40%. The report gives the tonnes and loads by crop and by month, the top five farms, the mean moisture by crop (and how many values were missing), the loads by crop over the co-operative's drying threshold of 14.5% moisture, and a data-quality section. Check yourself: these rules give 166 rows read, 6 duplicates removed, 6 rows rejected and 154 loads kept, from 8 farms, totalling 3,343.7 t.
deliverables: clean_deliveries.py, run as python clean_deliveries.py deliveries_raw.csv, with its functions split across at least two modules, docstrings, and a main() guarded by if __name__ == '__main__'
clean_deliveries.csv and rejected.csv, written with csv.DictWriter, every rejected row with its reason
report.md: tonnes and loads by crop and by month, the top five farms, mean moisture by crop, loads over 14.5% by crop, and a data-quality section that accounts for every row read
Clear messages instead of tracebacks: exit code 1 for a missing input file, and a warning naming the line of any row that can't be read
A notebook that imports your module and checks the cleaning, such as the farm and crop spellings before and after, and runs from top to bottom
A README.md and a Git history of at least four commits, with a .gitignore

rubric.description: Small functions in modules, built-in data structures used well (sets for duplicates, dictionaries for counts and groups), docstrings, comments that explain why, and a README.

rubric.description: A missing file, a bad row or an unexpected value gives a clear message and the right exit code, never a traceback, and nothing is dropped without being reported.
